author: Philip K. Dick
date_display: If, April 1954 (Quinn Publishing Co.) — byline details confirmed by Dick himself in a 1975 letter to his agent
card_summary: In a post-war America where radiation has produced mutants — 'deeves' — the Department of Civic Anthropology hunts and euthanises them at birth; eighty-seven types have been catalogued and dealt with in sixty years.
page_summary:
In a post-war America where radiation has produced mutants — 'deeves' — the Department of Civic Anthropology hunts and euthanises them at birth; eighty-seven types have been catalogued and dealt with in sixty years. A DCA agent posing as a salesman traces the eighty-eighth to the Johnson farm outside Walnut Creek, where a family has concealed their eldest son for eighteen years. Cris Johnson is golden — skin, hair, eyes — beautiful, silent, and without language. He has never communicated with his family in eighteen years. He evades capture instantly, then gives himself up voluntarily. In the laboratory the DCA cannot kill him: he dodges lash-tube fire, then a machine firing on a deliberately randomised pattern, weaving between the beams. Brain analysis returns the answer nobody wanted. He has virtually no frontal lobe. He does not think, does not use symbols, is not a superior man but an animal with one highly developed faculty — he sees the future as others see the present, a fixed landscape of tableaux through which he moves along an inflexible path. Baines and Wisdom work out the implication: intelligence is a dead end, and they are the last of their line. Cris escapes his cell and goes not to an exit but to Anita Ferris's room. She holds a weapon on him and cannot use it, because he only came because he had already seen she would not. He hands the weapon back to her. She takes him past the guards on her own authority — and at the exit he abandons her and is gone. The closing exchange establishes the second faculty: the gold is plumage. He will be sheltered by whichever woman he meets, and he already knows he is irresistible. Wisdom hopes his characteristics are recessive. Baines says he would not bet on it.

**Why it matters.** The story's design is a bait and switch about what supersession would look like. Everyone in it — including the reader — expects homo superior to be a bigger brain: telepathy, perfect symbolisation, a better human. What arrives instead has no language and no interior life, and wins because a single physical sense makes deliberation unnecessary. Baines's formulation is the point: we will know homo superior by definition, because he will be the one we cannot kill. What the story does not do is make Cris sympathetic or even present; he is a hole in the middle of his own story, which is a deliberate and effective choice.

*Wisdom hopes the traits are recessive. Baines says he is making a good guess, and it will not be them.*

movements: The Walnut Creek lunch counter: mutant types catalogued in gossip, and the town's silence when the subject comes too close.
The Johnson farm: the agent's ruse, the family's terror, and Cris's voluntary surrender.
The laboratory: the failed killings, the randomised firing machine, and the brain analysis that inverts the threat.
The escape: Anita's room, the walk past the guards, and the abandonment.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving between the DCA men and — for one remarkable stretch — inside Cris's perception, which is rendered as a doll's house of rooms, tableaux and duplicated selves along a fixed path.
structure.notable_technique: The opening ten minutes are pure exposition disguised as diner conversation: eight strangers swapping mutant sightings, which establishes the world's rules, its casual cruelty, and the euphemism 'euthed' before the plot begins.

characters.name: Cris Johnson
characters.note: Eighteen, mute, without language or tools, and not a person in any sense the story's characters can use. The narration enters his perception once and finds no reasoning in it — only a fixed landscape already seen.

characters.name: Baines
characters.note: Poses as the salesman and later as a real-estate developer. Supplies the story's argument: superior survival is not superior man, and if there were another flood only fish would survive.

characters.name: Ed Wisdom
characters.note: Wants the thing killed within forty-eight hours whether they understand it or not. His hope at the end that the traits are recessive is the story's last piece of self-deception.

characters.name: Anita Ferris
characters.role: Director of the Semantics Agency, Class A
characters.note: The story's most difficult figure. She objects to the killing on aesthetic grounds, is overcome, and is then written off by Baines as the first of a procession. The narration gives her humiliation and does not examine it.

characters.name: Nat Johnson
characters.note: Has hidden his son for eighteen years and draws on the agent when the ruse fails.

characters.name: Jean and Dave Johnson
characters.note: Jean's line that he is a god come down to earth is the phrase the DCA people keep returning to.

settings.name: A lunch counter in Walnut Creek
settings.note: Where the world is established entirely through casual talk about killed children.

settings.name: The Johnson farm
settings.note: Eighteen years of concealment, and a family who describe their son as having no contact with them of any kind.

settings.name: The DCA Building
settings.note: A sealed structure with a euth stage, a randomised firing machine and a bar in the lobby.

motifs: Euphemism as policy: 'euthed', 'deeve', the birth inspection, the stamped wrist
Gold as plumage rather than divinity — the story's final reframing of its own central image
Seeing as against thinking: prediction so complete it removes the need for a frontal lobe
The fixed path: Cris's perception is a doll's house of rooms in which one self among many is the one he will be
Intelligence as an evolutionary dead end, stated outright by the characters

distinctive_terms.label: Roman
distinctive_terms.note: From the description of Cris as a gilded Roman monument.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: The file contains the sharpest negative judgement Dick made of any story in this corpus — and it sits alongside his having let a collection be named after it.

evidence.quote: And maybe drop out "The Golden Man," which I detest?
evidence.reading: Proposing anthology contents. In the same breath he argues for including 'Second Variety' as one of his best. The judgement is unambiguous and unprompted.

evidence.source: Selected Letters — to Ralph Vicinanza, 23 February 1975
evidence.quote: "The Golden Man." If magazine, April, 1954 (Quinn Publishing Co.)
evidence.reading: Dick supplying copyright byline details to his agent for the British rights. Establishes the publication facts from his own hand.
The 1980 collection, named for the story he had said he detested, and for which he wrote a substantial introduction.

criticism.summary: Critics cite the 1980 volume's introduction far more often than the story, because that introduction is one of only two late autobiographical pieces Dick wrote.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: Phil had recently written two autobiographical pieces-the introduction to the Golden Man story collection and a short reminiscence on "Roog," his fir…
evidence.reading: Pairs this introduction with the 'Roog' reminiscence as the two late autobiographical statements. Both bear directly on other dossiers in this set.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: It reappeared in the 1980 "Introduction" to The Golden Man.
evidence.reading: Sutin treats the introduction as a source that recycles earlier self-narration — specifically the poverty and horsemeat anecdote — and notes Dick was no longer in want by 1978. A caution about the introduction's reliability as testimony.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: problems, replicating like mutants (or literally as mutants, as in "The Golden Man", 1954, CS3)
evidence.reading: Palmer uses the story as an instance of a general pattern rather than reading it in itself.

evidence.author: Anne R. Dick
evidence.work: The Search for Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: "The Golden Man" can see a halfhour ahead and can always find a woman to ke…
evidence.reading: Her summary names both faculties, including the second one, which most accounts of the story omit.

contradictions.summary: Dick asks an editor to drop the story because he detests it, and then permits a collection to be titled after it and writes its introduction.

claim_a.text: maybe drop out "The Golden Man," which I detest?

claim_b.text: a long autobiographical introduction to the collection named for it

contradictions.note: Not necessarily a change of view — a title is a publisher's decision and an introduction is paid work. But the file should not present either statement without the other.

open_questions: The 1980 introduction is not in the archive as a separate text. Sutin treats it as a major late autobiographical statement, and it is the obvious place to find whether Dick's stated detestation persisted. Worth acquiring.
Dick detested this story and rated 'Second Variety' among his best in the same letter. Does he anywhere give reasons for either judgement?
The story's brain-analysis conceit — supersession by something with no frontal lobe — is unusual in Dick. Does it recur anywhere, or is it isolated to 1954?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

later_use: Title story of the 1980 collection The Golden Man, for which Dick wrote a long autobiographical introduction.
